  of the source with its version or vintage, how and when the data were obtained (e.g.

  conditions others can obtain the same data. Where possible, identifiers or checksums
  let a user confirm they hold identical data.'

## Rating

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple" title="Met"}
Every data source used in the analysis is cited with its version or vintage (or a persistent identifier such as a DOI) and mapped to the corresponding files in the replication package. For data that cannot be shared (e.g. proprietary or confidential data), the README states how, where, and under what conditions an independent researcher can obtain the original source data, including any restrictions, requirements, payments, and processing delays. For data collected via an API or web scraping, the README also states the API or query used, the date of collection, and the configuration settings.

[Supported by: Access info for non-shareable data: [#42](../../sources.qmd#p42 "AEA data and code availability policy") (how, where, conditions, restrictions, payments, delays), [#95](../../sources.qmd#p95 "Computational reproducibility in finance: evidence from 1,000 tests") R1 (provider, DOI, vintage, application procedure), [#43](../../sources.qmd#p43 "Dawning of a new age? Economics journals’ data policies on the test bench"), [#105](../../sources.qmd#p105 "Promoting reproducibility and replicability in political science"), [#138](../../sources.qmd#p138 "Reproducibility and robustness of economics and political science research"), [#71](../../sources.qmd#p71 "Teaching for Large-Scale Reproducibility Verification"), [#54](../../sources.qmd#p54 "WORCS: a workflow for open reproducible code in science"). API/scraped data: [#108](../../sources.qmd#p108 "Checklists for computational reproducibility in social sciences: insights from literature and survey evaluation") (API, date, configuration), [#89](../../sources.qmd#p89 "Computational reproducibility in computational social science") (API version), [#34](../../sources.qmd#p34 "Reproducibility and replicability in economics"), [#26](../../sources.qmd#p26 "Facilitating reproducible project management and manuscript development in team science: the projects R package") 'frozen' dataset. PID: [#55](../../sources.qmd#p55 "Computational reproducibility: a practical framework for data curators"), [#65](../../sources.qmd#p65 "Long-term availability of data associated with articles in PLOS ONE"), [#110](../../sources.qmd#p110 "Data and code availability in political science publications from 1995 to 2022"), [#70](../../sources.qmd#p70 "The Stark realities of reproducible statistically orientated sociological research: Some newer rules of the sociological method").]{.source-note}
:::
::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple" title="Partially met"}
Data sources are cited, but the information is incomplete: e.g. some sources are not cited, the version/vintage or identifier is missing, or the access conditions for non-shareable data or the collection details for API-extracted data are only partly given.

[Supported by: [#14](../../sources.qmd#p14 "An empirical analysis of journal policy effectiveness for computational reproducibility") (79% cite all data; 70% give data location), [#30](../../sources.qmd#p30 "Advancing computational reproducibility in the dataverse data repository platform") personal-website deposits lack persistent citation, [#63](../../sources.qmd#p63 "Toward practical transparent verifiable and long-term reproducible research using guix") no integrity check on repository, [#102](../../sources.qmd#p102 "In-Class Data Analysis Replications: Teaching Students While Testing Science") outdated API.]{.source-note}
:::
::: {.callout-important appearance="simple" title="Not met"}
No provenance information available.

[Supported by: [#34](../../sources.qmd#p34 "Reproducibility and replicability in economics") query/revision of database cannot be determined, [#6](../../sources.qmd#p6 "A manifesto for data sharing in social media research") data not referenceable.]{.source-note}
:::


::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" title="Not applicable"}
A replication package is a simulation study (C1)
:::

**[#131](../../sources.qmd#p131)** Guide for Accelerating Computational Reproducibility in the Social Sciences · *injunctive*

> In the paper you chose, find references to all data sources used in the analysis. A data source is usually described in narrative form. For example, if in the body of the paper, or the appendix, you see text like “(…) for earnings in 2018 we use the Current Population Survey”, the data source should be recorded as “2018 Current Population Survey”. If the first reference to this data source is found on page 1 of the appendix, you should record its location as “A1”. Do this for all data sources mentioned in the paper. Each row represents a unique data source.
>
> Data sources also vary by unit of analysis, with some sources matching the same unit of analysis used in the paper (as in previous examples). In contrast, others may be less clear, e.g., “our information on regional minimum wages comes from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.” You should record such data source as “regional minimum wages from the Bureau of Labor Statistics.”
>
> Next, look at the reproduction package and map the data sources mentioned in the paper to the data files in the reproduction package. In the Location column, record their folder locations relative to the main reproduction folder1. In addition to looking at the existing data files, we recommend that you also review the first lines of all code files (especially cleaning code), looking for lines that call the datasets. Inspecting these scripts may help you understand how different data sources are used, and possibly identify any missing files from the reproduction package. Whenever a data source contains multiple files, enter them in the same cell, separated by semicolon (;).
